`edge_api()` turns a local GGUF model into an HTTP API that follows the
OpenAI chat completions format. One R process loads the model once and
answers many users. This vignette shows how to run it on your own machine,
how to deploy it to Posit Connect, and how to call it from R, ellmer and
Python.

The code in this vignette is not run when the package is built, because it
needs a model file and a running server.

## How it works

`edge_api()` loads the model and starts an engine (see `edge_engine()`).
The engine has `n_slots` slots. Each slot generates one answer, and all
busy slots move forward together, one token per step. Requests that find
every slot busy wait in a queue, first come first served, up to
`max_queue` requests. A busy server answers later. It only fails, with
status 503 and a `Retry-After` header, when the queue is full.

The request handlers return promises, so R keeps accepting new requests
while the model works.

## Running it locally

You need the plumber, jsonlite, promises and later packages.

```{r}
library(edgemodelr)

model <- "gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf"   # any chat model in GGUF format
api <- edge_api(model, n_slots = 4, n_ctx = 2048, api_key = "secret-key")
plumber::pr_run(api, host = "127.0.0.1", port = 8080)
```

`pr_run()` blocks the R session. Run it in its own R process (a second
terminal, a background job in RStudio, or `callr::r_bg()`), and call the
API from another one.

`edge_serve()` does the same in one call and prints the endpoints. Its
default is a single slot, which suits one user:

```{r}
edge_serve(model, port = 8080)
```

The main arguments of `edge_api()`:

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `n_slots` | 8 | Answers generated at the same time. |
| `n_ctx` | 2048 | Tokens per slot, prompt and answer together. |
| `n_threads` | one per core | CPU threads. `EDGEMODELR_THREADS` overrides it. |
| `max_queue` | 256 | Requests that may wait for a slot. |
| `cache_type` | `"q8_0"` | KV cache type. `"f16"` uses twice the memory. |
| `embeddings` | `FALSE` | `TRUE`, or the path of an embedding model, adds `POST /v1/embeddings`. |
| `api_key` | none | Key that clients must send. |
| `model_name` | file name | Name reported in replies and `/v1/models`. |

`n_slots * n_ctx` may be at most 32768 tokens.

## Endpoints

| Method | Path | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| POST | `/v1/chat/completions` | Chat completion, with `tools`, `response_format` and `stream`. |
| POST | `/v1/completions` | Text completion. |
| POST | `/v1/jobs` | Starts a chat completion in the background. Returns 202 and a job id. |
| GET | `/v1/jobs/<id>` | Status, queue position and text so far, then the full response. |
| DELETE | `/v1/jobs/<id>` | Cancels a job. |
| POST | `/v1/embeddings` | Only when `embeddings` is set. |
| GET | `/v1/models` | The model name. |
| GET | `/metrics` | Engine counters. |
| GET | `/health` | Status and slot use. Needs no key. |

Requests take `max_tokens` (or `max_completion_tokens`), `temperature`,
`top_p`, `top_k`, `min_p`, `repeat_penalty`, `seed` and `stop`.

With `stream = true` the reply comes as server-sent events in the OpenAI
chunk format. The chunks are sent together when the answer is finished,
so a client gets the format but does not see the text as it is written.
Use jobs to show text while it is written.

## Authentication

When `api_key` is set, every endpoint except `/health` needs one of these
headers:

```
Authorization: Bearer <key>
X-API-Key: <key>
```

A request without a valid key gets status 401. On Posit Connect, use
`X-API-Key`, because Connect uses the `Authorization` header for its own
keys. You can also leave `api_key` unset and use Connect's access
settings instead.

## Calling it from R

With httr2:

```{r}
library(httr2)

base <- "http://127.0.0.1:8080"
key <- "secret-key"

resp <- request(paste0(base, "/v1/chat/completions")) |>
  req_auth_bearer_token(key) |>
  req_body_json(list(
    messages = list(
      list(role = "system", content = "Answer in one sentence."),
      list(role = "user", content = "What is R?")
    ),
    max_tokens = 60,
    temperature = 0
  )) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

resp$choices[[1]]$message$content
resp$usage$completion_tokens
```

With the curl package:

```{r}
h <- curl::new_handle()
curl::handle_setheaders(h,
  "Content-Type" = "application/json",
  "X-API-Key" = key
)
curl::handle_setopt(h, postfields = jsonlite::toJSON(list(
  messages = list(list(role = "user", content = "Say hello.")),
  max_tokens = 20
), auto_unbox = TRUE))

out <- curl::curl_fetch_memory(paste0(base, "/v1/chat/completions"), handle = h)
reply <- jsonlite::fromJSON(rawToChar(out$content))
reply$choices$message$content
```

And from a shell:

```sh
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-API-Key: secret-key" \
  -d '{"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}], "max_tokens": 40}'
```

## Calling it from ellmer

`ellmer::chat_openai_compatible()` works against `<server>/v1`. The
`credentials` function returns the key, which ellmer sends as a Bearer
token:

```{r}
library(ellmer)

chat <- chat_openai_compatible(
  base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1",
  credentials = function() "secret-key",
  model = "gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M"
)
chat$chat("What is 2 + 2?")
```

To send `X-API-Key` instead, for example on Posit Connect, return a named
list of headers:

```{r}
chat <- chat_openai_compatible(
  base_url = "https://connect.example.com/content/<guid>/v1",
  credentials = function() list(`X-API-Key` = Sys.getenv("EDGEMODELR_API_KEY")),
  model = "gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M"
)
```

`chat_edge(base_url = )` also connects to a running server, but it cannot
send a key. Use it only with a server that has no `api_key`. See
`vignette("ellmer", package = "edgemodelr")`.

## Calling it from Python

The official OpenAI client works when `base_url` points at `/v1`. It sends
the key as a Bearer token:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1", api_key="secret-key")

reply = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is R?"}],
    max_tokens=60,
)
print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
```

On Posit Connect, send the API's key in `X-API-Key` with
`default_headers={"X-API-Key": "..."}`. The client still needs some
`api_key` value; any placeholder works when the content is open to
everyone.

## Jobs for Shiny apps

A plain chat request stays open until the whole answer is ready. With a
long queue that can take minutes, and proxies often cut requests after 60
seconds. Jobs avoid this. `POST /v1/jobs` takes the same body as a chat
completion and returns at once:

```{r}
job <- request(paste0(base, "/v1/jobs")) |>
  req_headers(`X-API-Key` = key) |>
  req_body_json(list(
    messages = list(list(role = "user", content = "Write two sentences about rivers.")),
    max_tokens = 80
  )) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()

job$id
job$status   # "queued"
```

Then poll `GET /v1/jobs/<id>`. While the job waits, the reply has
`status = "queued"` and `queue_position`. While it runs, it has
`status = "running"` and the text so far in `text`. When it is done,
`status` is `"done"` and `response` holds the full chat completion.

```{r}
repeat {
  j <- request(paste0(base, "/v1/jobs/", job$id)) |>
    req_headers(`X-API-Key` = key) |>
    req_perform() |>
    resp_body_json()
  if (j$status %in% c("done", "error", "cancelled")) break
  Sys.sleep(0.5)
}
j$response$choices[[1]]$message$content
```

`DELETE /v1/jobs/<id>` cancels a job and frees its slot. Finished jobs
are kept for 15 minutes.

In a Shiny app, start the job in an `observeEvent()` and poll it in an
`observe()` with `invalidateLater(500)`. Cancel the job in
`session$onSessionEnded()`, so a user who closes the page frees the slot.
`inst/examples/posit-connect/shiny/app.R` is a complete chat app built
this way:

```{r}
system.file("examples", "posit-connect", package = "edgemodelr")
```

## Timings

Chat and text completions include a `timings` object, in the form
llama.cpp's server uses. A stream has it on its last chunk.

| Field | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `queue_ms` | Time waiting for a free slot. |
| `prompt_n` | Prompt tokens. |
| `prompt_cached_n` | Prompt tokens reused from a slot. |
| `prompt_ms` | Time reading the prompt. |
| `first_token_ms` | Time from arrival to the first token. |
| `predicted_n` | Tokens generated. |
| `predicted_ms` | Time generating after the first token. |
| `predicted_per_second` | Generation speed for this request. |
| `total_ms` | Time from arrival to the end. |

```{r}
resp$timings$queue_ms
resp$timings$predicted_per_second
```

A slot keeps its tokens after an answer. A new request that starts the
same way, with the same system prompt or the next turn of a chat, skips
that part of its prompt. `prompt_cached_n` and
`usage$prompt_tokens_details$cached_tokens` show how many tokens it
skipped.

If `queue_ms` is large, the server needs more slots or more CPU. If
`predicted_per_second` is low while `queue_ms` is small, the CPU is the
limit.

## Metrics and health

`GET /health` needs no key, so a load balancer or Connect can use it:

```{r}
request(paste0(base, "/health")) |> req_perform() |> resp_body_json()
# status "ok", model, slots, active, queued
```

`GET /metrics` returns the engine's counters: `slots`, `active`, `queued`,
`max_queue`, `n_ctx`, `requests_done`, `requests_failed`,
`requests_cancelled`, `tokens_generated`, `tokens_prompt`,
`tokens_reused`, `busy_seconds`, `uptime_seconds` and
`tokens_per_second` (total generated tokens per busy second).

```{r}
m <- request(paste0(base, "/metrics")) |>
  req_headers(`X-API-Key` = key) |>
  req_perform() |>
  resp_body_json()
m$tokens_per_second
```

## Slots, the queue and CPU sizing

On a CPU, more slots give more tokens per second in total, until the
cores are busy. That is usually at about 8 slots. Beyond that each answer
gets slower and the total barely grows. On an 8 core laptop, Gemma 3 1B
went from 13 tokens per second with 1 slot to 44 to 54 with 8 slots.

Each slot reserves `n_ctx` tokens of KV cache, so memory is the model
file plus `n_slots * n_ctx` tokens of cache. For Gemma 3 1B (Q4_K_M) with
8 slots of 2048 tokens that is about 0.8 GB for the model and 0.3 GB for
the cache.

On a CPU-only container:

- Give the API whole cores. The engine uses one thread per core.
- Inside a container, the default thread count follows the container's
  CPU limit (cgroup v1 or v2), not the host's core count. Set
  `n_threads` or `EDGEMODELR_THREADS` only if that guess is wrong.
- More cores shorten the wait almost linearly. More slots than about 8
  add little.
- Wait time grows with the number of users waiting. Nobody gets an error
  until the queue is full, so set `max_queue` to the most users you
  expect at once.

## Deploying to Posit Connect

`inst/examples/posit-connect/` has two pieces of content:

- `api/entrypoint.R`, a plumber API that calls `edge_api()` and returns
  the router. It reads its settings from environment variables.
- `shiny/app.R`, a chat app that never loads a model. It submits jobs to
  the API and polls them.

The entrypoint, shortened:

```{r}
library(edgemodelr)

env <- function(name, default = "") {
  value <- Sys.getenv(name)
  if (nzchar(value)) value else default
}

model <- env("EDGEMODELR_MODEL")
if (!nzchar(model) || !file.exists(model)) {
  model <- edge_download_model(
    env("EDGEMODELR_MODEL_REPO", "unsloth/gemma-3-1b-it-GGUF"),
    env("EDGEMODELR_MODEL_FILE", "gemma-3-1b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf"),
    cache_dir = env("EDGEMODELR_CACHE_DIR", tools::R_user_dir("edgemodelr", "cache")),
    trust_first_use = TRUE
  )
}

edge_api(
  model,
  n_slots = as.integer(env("EDGEMODELR_SLOTS", "8")),
  n_ctx = as.integer(env("EDGEMODELR_CTX", "2048")),
  max_queue = 512L,
  api_key = env("EDGEMODELR_API_KEY")
)
```

An empty `api_key` means no key.

Deploy the two folders:

```{r}
rsconnect::deployAPI("api", appTitle = "Local model API")
rsconnect::deployApp("shiny", appTitle = "Local model chat")
```

Connect installs the packages your local library records, so install
edgemodelr the same way you want Connect to install it before you deploy.

### Settings for the API

Vars:

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `EDGEMODELR_MODEL` | Path of a .gguf file on a persistent volume. Or leave it unset to download. |
| `EDGEMODELR_MODEL_REPO`, `EDGEMODELR_MODEL_FILE` | Hugging Face repo and file to download on first start. |
| `EDGEMODELR_CACHE_DIR` | A persistent path for the download. Each deploy starts in a fresh folder. |
| `EDGEMODELR_SLOTS` | Answers generated at once (default 8). |
| `EDGEMODELR_CTX` | Tokens per answer, prompt included (default 2048). |
| `EDGEMODELR_THREADS` | CPU threads, if the default is wrong. |
| `EDGEMODELR_API_KEY` | Optional. Clients send it as `X-API-Key`. |

Runtime:

| Setting | Value | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Min processes | 1 | Keeps the model loaded. A cold start loads it again. |
| Max processes | 1 | Each process loads its own copy of the model. One process with many slots uses the CPU better than several processes. |
| Max connections per process | 200 | The default, 20, makes Connect start a second process, and a second model, at about 11 users. |
| Load factor | 1.0 | The default, 0.5, makes Connect start processes early. |
| Initial timeout | 600 | Time to download and load the model on first start. |
| Idle timeout | 3600 or more | Keeps the process, and the model, between bursts of use. |
| Read timeout | 3600 | A long queue can keep a plain chat request open for minutes. Jobs avoid this. |

If a proxy or load balancer sits in front of Connect, check its own read
timeout as well. `POST /v1/chat/completions` waits for the whole answer,
`POST /v1/jobs` does not.

### Settings for the Shiny app

Set `EDGEMODELR_API_URL` to the API's content URL, such as
`https://connect.example.com/content/<guid>`, and `EDGEMODELR_API_KEY` if
the API has a key. Connect gives the app its own `CONNECT_API_KEY`, which
the app sends as `Authorization: Key <key>` so it can reach an API whose
access is restricted. That key belongs to the app's owner, who must have
access to the API. The app can keep Connect's default runtime settings,
since it holds no model.

See `inst/examples/posit-connect/README.md` for measurements with 50
users at once.
